notes.text: For more than 8, brown the chicken in three batches and use your biggest pot, so the pieces fit in one or two layers for the braise.

callback.body: In chana masala you cooked spices in hot oil for a minute so their flavor bloomed. A tagine starts the same way. The new part is what comes after: a lid, a little liquid, and slow, gentle heat.

move.title: Brown, bloom, braise
move.body: A tagine is a Moroccan stew named for the clay pot it's cooked in, though any heavy pot with a lid works. Today you'll brown chicken thighs, cook onion and spices in the same pot, then add a little broth, put the lid on, and let the chicken braise gently until it's tender. Lemon and green olives go in at the end.

why.title: Brown first for flavor
why.body: Browning the chicken makes a deep golden crust and leaves brown bits stuck to the pot. Those bits are pure flavor, and the broth lifts them up into the sauce later.

why.title: Bloom the spices
why.body: Spice flavor dissolves in fat. Stirring the ground spices into the hot oil and onion for a minute, before any liquid goes in, makes them taste warm and full instead of dusty.

why.title: A braise is gentle
why.body: Braising means cooking in a little liquid with the lid on, over low heat. The steam and the broth cook the chicken slowly, so it turns tender and soaks up the sauce.

why.title: Small bubbles only
why.body: A hard boil toughens chicken. Keep the heat low enough that only a few small bubbles rise around the edges of the pot.

why.title: Olives and lemon at the end
why.body: Olives turn bitter and lemon loses its fresh taste if they cook too long. Stirred in for the last few minutes, they stay bright and salty-sour.

wrong.fix: The heat was too high. Pour in the broth right away to stop them cooking, and keep going.

wrong.sign: The sauce is thin and watery
wrong.fix: Take the lid off and simmer 5 more minutes, until it thickens.
The olives are salty. Add a splash of water and an extra squeeze of lemon.
Put the lid back on and braise 5 more minutes, then check again.

choices: Cooking slowly in a little liquid with the lid on
quiz.explain: Steam and broth cook it gently.

quiz.q: Why do the spices go into the oil before the broth?
When do the olives go in?

steps.text: Halve the onions and slice them into thin half-moons. Peel and mince the garlic, and grate the ginger.
steps.tip: Hold the food with your hand shaped like a claw: fingertips tucked under, knuckles in front.

steps.text: Measure the cumin, paprika, turmeric, cinnamon, and pepper into the small bowl.
steps.tip: Turmeric stains. Wipe up spills right away.

steps.text: Pat the chicken dry with paper towels, lay it on the plate, and sprinkle both sides with the salt.
Throw the paper towels away. Wash your hands with soap, and wipe anything the raw chicken touched.
Heat the oil in the large pot over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Use the tongs to lay half the chicken in the pot. Leave it until the bottom is golden, then turn it and brown the other side. Move it back to the plate and brown the rest.
steps.look: Golden brown on both sides. It doesn't need to be cooked through yet.

steps.text: Put the tongs in the sink and wash your hands. Use the wooden spoon from here on.
Turn the heat to medium. Add the onions to the pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden.
steps.look: Soft, golden onions, picking up the brown bits.

steps.text: Add the garlic, ginger, and spices. Stir for 1 minute.
steps.look: It smells warm and toasty, and the onions turn deep yellow.

steps.text: Pour in the broth and scrape the bottom of the pot with the wooden spoon. Put the chicken and its juices back in.
steps.tip: Pour slowly. The steam rushes up.

steps.text: Rinse the rice, then bring it to a boil with the water in the saucepan. Cover, turn to low, and cook. Leave it covered off the heat until serving.
Put the lid on the large pot and turn the heat to low. Braise, turning the chicken once halfway.
steps.look: Small bubbles around the edge, not a rolling boil.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer into the thickest piece of chicken. It needs to read at least 165°F. If it doesn't, cover it and braise 5 more minutes.
Squeeze in the lemon juice and add the olives. Simmer with the lid off until the sauce thickens a little.
Turn off the stove. Spoon the chicken and sauce over the rice and scatter the cilantro on top.

season.text: Pat the chicken dry with paper towels and season it with the salt.

wash-season.text: Throw the paper towels away and wash your hands.

brown.text: Heat the oil in the pot over medium heat. Brown the chicken skin side down in two batches with the tongs, then turn and brown briefly. Set the pieces aside.

wash-brown.text: Put the tongs in the sink and wash your hands. Use clean tongs from here.

onions-in.text: Cook the onions in the fat until soft and golden, scraping up the brown bits.

bloom.text: Add the garlic, ginger, and spices and stir for 1 minute.

broth.text: Add the broth and the zest strips, scrape the pot clean, and return the chicken skin side up with its juices.

rice.text: Rinse the rice and bring it to a boil with the water in the saucepan. Cover, cook on low, and hold it off the heat, covered.

braise.text: Cover and braise on low, with only small bubbles at the edge.

finish.text: Return the breasts. Add the olives and the lemon juice, and simmer uncovered until the sauce coats a spoon. Season to taste.

serve.text: Serve over the rice with the cilantro.

add.text: Weigh the chicken in its wrapping, then unwrap it over the board. Don't rinse it.

Break the chicken into 8 pieces: legs off at the hip joint, then split at the knee; wings off at the shoulder; the breast off the back, then halved through the breastbone. Cut the back into 2 pieces for stock.
add.look: Two each of drumsticks, thighs, wings, and breast halves, plus the back.

add.text: Bag the back and freeze it for stock. Wash your hands, the knife, and the board with hot, soapy water.
Slice the onions into thin half-moons, mince the garlic, grate the ginger, and peel the lemon zest in wide strips. Measure the spices into the small bowl.
Pour off all but 2 tablespoons of the fat into the heatproof bowl.
Check the breasts: at least 165°F. Move them to the plate and cover them.
Braise the dark meat 10 to 15 minutes longer, until a thigh reads about 185°F and is tender at the bone.
Check the thickest thigh: at least 165°F, and tender.

move.title: One bird, eight pieces, one pot
move.body: Moroccan tagine from a whole chicken: you break the bird into eight pieces, brown them skin side down, bloom the spices in the rendered fat, and braise everything with lemon zest and broth. The breasts come out at 165°F; the dark meat stays in until it's tender. The back goes to the freezer for stock.

wrong.sign: The skin is pale and flabby
wrong.fix: Brown longer before turning, over medium heat, and don't crowd the pot.
Tilt the pot and spoon off the fat that pools at the edge.
They stayed in past 165°F. Next time, check them first and pull them early.
Braise them 10 to 15 minutes longer. Dark meat softens as it nears 185°F.

quiz.q: Why do the breasts come out of the braise first?
choices: White meat dries out past 165°F; dark meat gets more tender
quiz.explain: Each part is cooked to what suits it.

quiz.q: Why pour off most of the rendered fat?
choices: Too much makes the sauce greasy

quiz.q: What stands in for preserved lemon here?
choices: Wide strips of fresh zest simmered in the sauce
quiz.explain: The peel's oil carries the perfume.

add.title: Eight pieces
add.body: Two drumsticks, two thighs, two wings, and two breast halves, each cut so the bone stays with its meat. Pieces of similar size braise in the same time; the breasts, leanest, are the one exception.

add.title: Render, then pour off
add.body: Chicken skin browned slowly gives up its fat. Keep about 2 tablespoons to cook the onions and spices in, and pour the rest off: too much, and the sauce turns greasy.

add.title: Breasts out first
add.body: White meat is done at 165°F and dries out past it. Dark meat has more connective tissue and gets more tender as it keeps braising, up to about 185°F. Pull the breasts when they're done, and put them back to warm at the end.

add.title: Zest for preserved lemon
add.body: Moroccan cooks use preserved lemon, salted for weeks until the peel goes soft. Wide strips of fresh zest simmered in the sauce give a similar perfume from the peel's oil; the juice goes in at the end for brightness.
